testing: How many issues did testing catch?

13: four unknown material patterns; the brainstorm reading its layout only from draw (dead input headless); the attract autopilot stuck on furniture; a window hotspot overlapping the typewriter; the pixel font missing the PlayStation symbols (prompts showed '?'); a missing middle dot; card text overflowing; suits drawn as white shirts; the pitch camera hiding the clients behind the HUD and chairs; no AI Hub progress reports during play (harness fail); garbled icons in the tiny font; the wrong hint on touch-only screens; the logo crowding the corner button on portrait phones.
How many would be considered critical issues / game breaking?

3: the missing PlayStation glyphs (every controller prompt unreadable), the missing hub progress reports (the hub would keep the game out of sessions), and the pitch camera hiding the client you are pitching to.
What was the most helpful test you ran?

The headless three-day playthrough in Node (94 checks): it drives every conversation, card, event, pitch, ending and mode in seconds and caught the input and hotspot bugs; a close second is the AI Hub harness, which caught the missing progress reports.
What was the least helpful test you ran?
The viewport matrix on the title screen: all 24 sizes came back clean, so it mostly confirmed the engine's expand layout, though its phone shots did show the logo crowding the corner button.
engine: What did you like most about the engine?

How much comes for free and works the same everywhere: the pause menu, settings, rebinding, glyph families, saves, dialog with live portraits, lighting, and an exact fixed-step clock that makes a whole game testable headless in Node.
Did you get stuck or guess wrong?

A few times: material shorthand patterns (leather, velvet, leaves and marble are not patterns), the 'coat' outfit using cloth for the torso, the font lacking the PlayStation symbols its own input labels return, and the side view's depth for props.
What was the most important thing you had to build yourself?

The pitch system (cards with angles, client wants that change mid-pitch, the timing meter, pivots and the beat-timed close), plus Simlish voices driven from the dialog's typing, the clock-and-events office day, and the gamepad axis-inversion fix.
What was the hardest part about using the engine?

Finding the right names in a very large API: the index helps, but details like which views a prop faces in, how mouseGround returns, or that FlowField ignores placed furniture needed reading the source or trial and error.
If you had to remove or overhaul one thing from engine, what woudl that be?

The material shorthand's silent fallback: an unknown pattern only warns once in the console, so a typo quietly changes how furniture looks; it should fail loudly or list the patterns at the call site.
If you could change one thing about the engine, what would it be?
Ship the PlayStation and Xbox button symbols in the pixel fonts, since input.label() returns them, and add a public font.define() for game glyphs; also make FlowField avoid map.solid furniture.
prompt: What did you like most about this prompt?
It is concrete about what done means: attract mode timing, controller-first UI with glyph and inversion settings, touch-only behaviour, hub integration, and a full feedback loop.

The deliverable name pattern (how to write GameTitle and SOURCE in a file name with spaces and a year), and whether 'multiplayer for the game on its own' meant local multiplayer as well as the hub; I did both.
What was the hardest thing to do?
Turning a slow, talky drama into a game loop with real decisions: the insight cards, the clock and composure trade-offs and the timed pitch had to make persuasion feel like play.
If there was one test you could of run, what would that test be?
A real DualSense on a TV at ten feet with a person playing all three days, to judge readability, pacing and whether the pitch meter feels fair; I could only mock the gamepad in the browser.
